title: Type Conversions & Casting
summary: Go has **no implicit numeric conversions** — you must write `T(v)` explicitly, even between `int` and `int64`. This strictness eliminates a whole class of C-style bugs, but it also means you need to understand truncation, overflow, and the famous `string(65)` gotcha to convert values correctly.

subtopics.title: Explicit conversion T(v)
subtopics.explanation: Go never converts numeric types implicitly. To use an int where an int64 is expected you must write the conversion yourself: int64(x). The compiler rejects mixing types, which catches accidental data-truncation bugs at compile time rather than at runtime.
subtopics.example: var i int = 5; var f float64 = float64(i)

subtopics.title: int <-> float64 truncates
subtopics.explanation: Converting a float to an int truncates toward zero — it does NOT round. So int(2.9) is 2 and int(-2.9) is -2. Converting int to float64 is exact for small magnitudes but can lose precision for very large integers.

subtopics.title: Narrowing overflows predictably
subtopics.explanation: Converting a wide integer to a narrower one keeps only the low bits — well-defined two's-complement truncation, not undefined behavior. int8(300) wraps to 44. Always check range before narrowing untrusted values.

subtopics.title: string(n) is the rune gotcha
subtopics.explanation: string(65) is "A", not "65" — converting an integer to a string interprets it as a Unicode code point. To get the decimal text use strconv.Itoa(65). Modern Go vet even warns about int-to-string conversions.

subtopics.title: []byte / []rune copy the data
subtopics.explanation: []byte(s) and []rune(s) allocate a new slice and copy, because strings are immutable. string([]byte{...}) round-trips back. These conversions are not free — avoid them in hot loops.

subtopics.title: Defined types & their underlying type
subtopics.explanation: A defined type like type Celsius float64 is distinct from float64; you must convert explicitly between them (Celsius(t) / float64(c)) even though they share representation. This gives you type safety with no runtime cost.

foundations.overview: Many languages quietly convert one numeric type to another for you — an int becomes a double, a char becomes an int — and that convenience hides bugs. Go takes the opposite stance: it has NO implicit numeric conversions. If two values are of different types, you must convert one explicitly with the T(v) syntax. This lesson covers the rules: how numeric conversions truncate and overflow, why string(65) is a famous trap, and how strconv handles real number-to-text work.
foundations.formalDefinition: A conversion T(x) changes the type of an expression x to the type T when x is assignable to T or their underlying types are convertible. It is a compile-time, value-producing operation distinct from a type assertion, which is a runtime check on an interface value.
foundations.whyItMatters: Conversions sit at every boundary: parsing input, talking to databases, serializing JSON, doing math across types. Getting them wrong silently corrupts data — a truncated float, an overflowed counter, or a byte that turns into a Chinese character instead of '42'.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of each type as a labeled box of a fixed size. T(v) means 'take the bits in this box and reinterpret/repackage them into a T-shaped box.' Sometimes that fits perfectly (int to int64), sometimes it must drop bits (int64 to int8), and sometimes it reinterprets meaning entirely (int to string treats the number as a code point).
foundations.runtimePerspective: Most numeric conversions compile to a single machine instruction (sign-extend, zero-extend, or truncate) and are essentially free. But []byte(s), []rune(s), and string([]byte) allocate new memory and copy, because Go strings are immutable and the runtime must not let you mutate string-backing memory.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Reading an HTTP query param ('age=30') and turning it into an int with strconv.Atoi; converting a database int64 id into the int your API expects; building a []byte payload from a string to send over a socket.
foundations.businessImpact: An overflow on a money or quantity field that silently wraps can corrupt billing or inventory. Explicit conversions force engineers to acknowledge the boundary, reducing costly data-integrity incidents.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Go's no-implicit-conversion rule means type mismatches are compile errors, not runtime surprises. The cost is more verbose code; the benefit is that whole categories of C-style coercion bugs simply cannot happen.
foundations.performanceImpact: Numeric conversions are free, but []byte/[]rune conversions copy O(n) bytes and allocate. In tight loops, reuse buffers or avoid round-tripping strings to keep the garbage collector quiet.
commonUseCases: Parsing text input with strconv.Atoi / strconv.Itoa
Bridging int and int64 at API/DB boundaries
Building []byte payloads from strings for I/O
Defining domain types (type UserID int64) for safety

commonMisconceptions.reality: It gives the rune for code point 42 (a control character). Use strconv.Itoa(42) for the decimal text "42".
Numeric conversions are cheap, but []byte(s), []rune(s), and string([]byte) allocate and copy the data because strings are immutable.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Converting a float to an int rounds it.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It truncates toward zero: int(2.9) is 2 and int(-2.9) is -2. Use math.Round first if you want rounding.

visualExplorer.title: How a conversion T(v) flows
visualExplorer.caption: Follow a value as it crosses type boundaries: numeric widening, truncation, the rune trap, and strconv for real text.

config.intro: Go forces every cross-type move through an explicit T(v). Walk through what each kind of conversion actually does to the bits.

steps.name: 1. Widening: int to int64
steps.detail: int64(x) sign-extends the value into a wider box. No data is lost; the compiler still requires you to write it explicitly.

steps.name: 2. float to int truncates
steps.detail: int(2.9) drops the fractional part toward zero, giving 2. There is no rounding — math.Round(2.9) would be needed first to get 3.

steps.name: 3. Narrowing overflows
steps.detail: int8(300) keeps only the low 8 bits, wrapping to 44 by two's-complement truncation. Range-check untrusted values before narrowing.

steps.name: 4. The string(n) rune trap
steps.detail: string(65) reinterprets 65 as a Unicode code point and yields "A", not "65". For decimal text you must use strconv.Itoa.

steps.name: 5. strconv for text <-> number
steps.detail: strconv.Atoi("42") parses text into an int (with an error); strconv.Itoa(42) formats an int back into "42". This is the correct number<->string bridge.

interactiveExamples.title: Truncation, overflow, and the rune trap
interactiveExamples.explanation: Three classic surprises in one program: float-to-int truncates (not rounds), narrowing wraps, and string(n) gives a rune — not the digits.

code.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	f := 2.9
	fmt.Println(int(f))          // truncates toward zero -> 2

	big := 300
	fmt.Println(int8(big))       // keeps low 8 bits -> 44 (wraps)

	fmt.Println(string(rune(65))) // code point 65 -> "A", NOT "65"
}

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: print "42", not a strange symbol
interactiveExamples.explanation: string(n) interprets n as a Unicode code point, so string(42) is a control character, not "42". Edit the code to print the decimal text using strconv.

checkpoints.explanation: Float-to-int conversion truncates toward zero, dropping the fractional part. -2.9 becomes -2, not -3. Rounding would require math.Round first.
string(rune(n)) converts a code point to its character: 72 is 'H' and 105 is 'i', so the result is "Hi". This is exactly why string(intVal) does NOT give you the decimal digits.

checkpoints.prompt: How do you correctly turn the int 255 into the string "255"?
checkpoints.explanation: strconv.Itoa formats an int as its decimal text. string(255) would give the rune for code point 255 ('y' with diaeresis), and []byte(255) does not compile.

debuggingLab.title: Converting an int to a string gives a weird symbol
debuggingLab.symptom: The program is supposed to log "order #42" but prints "order #*" (or some other odd character) instead of the number.

brokenCode.code:
id := 42
msg := "order #" + string(rune(id)) // intended to append "42"
fmt.Println(msg)

debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: string(rune(id)) converts the integer to the Unicode character at that code point. Code point 42 is '*', so you get "order #*" instead of "order #42". Converting an int directly to a string never produces its decimal digits.
commonMistakes: Using string(intVal) (or string(rune(intVal))) expecting the decimal text.
Forgetting that strconv (or fmt.Sprintf) is the tool for number-to-text formatting.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Format the integer as decimal text with strconv.Itoa before concatenating.

solution.code:
import "strconv"

id := 42
msg := "order #" + strconv.Itoa(id) // Itoa -> "42"
fmt.Println(msg)

theory.question: Why does Go require explicit conversions like int64(x) even between integer types?
theory.directAnswer: Go has no implicit numeric conversions by design. Different numeric types are genuinely different types, and Go refuses to silently widen or narrow them because that's where C-style truncation and sign bugs hide. Forcing T(v) makes every boundary visible and turns potential runtime data loss into a compile-time decision.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A language rule that values of different types — even int and int64 — cannot be mixed in expressions or assigned without an explicit conversion.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To eliminate the implicit coercions that cause silent precision loss and overflow bugs in languages like C.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The compiler checks types statically; a mismatch is an error, and the only way through is an explicit conversion the programmer writes.

theory.whyImportant: It's a core philosophy question that reveals whether a candidate understands Go's safety-through-explicitness trade-off.
theory.realWorldExample: A database driver returns int64 ids; converting to int with int(id) makes the truncation risk on 32-bit platforms explicit instead of silent.

followUps.question: Is int64(x) free at runtime?
followUps.answer: For widening it's a single sign-extend instruction, effectively free. Narrowing is also cheap but may lose high bits.

followUps.question: Does the same rule apply to untyped constants?
followUps.answer: No — untyped constants like 5 adapt to the context's type automatically, so var f float64 = 5 needs no conversion.

theory.question: What's the difference between a type conversion T(v) and a type assertion x.(T)?
theory.directAnswer: A conversion T(v) is a compile-time operation between statically compatible types (numbers, defined types, []byte/string) that always succeeds. A type assertion x.(T) is a runtime operation on an interface value that extracts the concrete type, can fail (panic, or return ok=false in the comma-ok form), and only applies to interfaces. They look similar but solve different problems.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Conversion repackages a known concrete type; assertion inspects what concrete type hides inside an interface.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Conversions bridge compatible representations; assertions recover static type info that was erased when a value was stored in an interface.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The compiler resolves conversions statically. Assertions check the interface's dynamic type descriptor at runtime.

theory.whyImportant: Confusing the two is common; interviewers use it to test understanding of Go's type system and interfaces (a separate topic, golang-intermediate-4).
theory.realWorldExample: float64(i) converts an int; v, ok := any.(string) asserts that an interface{} actually holds a string before using it.

followUps.question: What happens if a type assertion fails without the comma-ok form?
followUps.answer: It panics at runtime. Use the v, ok := x.(T) form to handle the failure gracefully.

scenario.question: A service reads a numeric count from an external system as int64, stores it in an int32 column-mapped field, and occasionally records show absurd negative counts. What's happening and how do you fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: The int64 is being narrowed to int32, and when the value exceeds the int32 range the conversion keeps only the low 32 bits via two's-complement truncation — which can flip the sign and produce a large negative number. The fix is to range-check before converting (reject or clamp values outside math.MinInt32..math.MaxInt32) or widen the field to int64.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Silent integer narrowing overflow at a type boundary.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Go defines narrowing as low-bit truncation, which is fast and predictable but lossy for out-of-range values.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: int32(largeInt64) discards the high bits; if bit 31 ends up set, the value is interpreted as negative.

scenario.whyImportant: Boundary narrowing is a real data-integrity bug class, especially with untrusted or growing external values.
scenario.realWorldExample: An event counter from a busy upstream exceeds 2.1 billion and wraps to a negative int32, corrupting dashboards and alerts.

followUps.question: How do you safely detect the overflow?
followUps.answer: Compare against math.MaxInt32/math.MinInt32 before converting, and return an error or clamp if out of range.

coding.question: Implement `func SumDigits(s string) (int, error)` that parses a string of digits like "12345" and returns the sum of its digit values, returning an error if the string isn't a valid integer.
coding.thoughtProcess: Parse the whole string to an int with strconv.Atoi (which returns an error for invalid input), then repeatedly take n%10 to peel off digits and n/=10 to shrink. Sum the remainders. Handle the empty/invalid case via the returned error.
coding.lineByLine: strconv.Atoi converts the text to an int and surfaces an error for non-numeric input. We take the absolute value so negatives still sum their digits. The loop pulls the last digit with %10, adds it, and divides by 10 to move on, stopping at 0. The error is propagated to the caller idiomatically.
coding.timeComplexity: O(d) where d is the number of digits

followUps.question: Why use strconv.Atoi instead of int(s)?
followUps.answer: int(s) doesn't compile — you can't convert a string to an int that way. strconv.Atoi is the correct text-to-number parser and reports invalid input.

followUps.question: How would you sum digits without parsing to int at all?
followUps.answer: Range over the string's runes and convert each digit rune with r - '0', validating each is between '0' and '9'.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Define domain types (type UserID int64, type Cents int64) so conversions become explicit boundaries; the compiler then prevents accidentally passing a price where an id is expected.
productionDeepDive.performance: Numeric conversions are free, but []byte(s)/[]rune(s)/string([]byte) copy and allocate. In hot paths, reuse buffers, prefer strconv.AppendInt over string concatenation, and avoid needless string<->[]byte round-trips.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: Conversions themselves are pure and goroutine-safe, but a []byte produced by converting a string is a fresh, mutable copy — sharing it across goroutines without synchronization is still a data race if it's written.
productionDeepDive.reliability: Range-check before narrowing untrusted integers (compare against math.MaxInt32 etc.) so a wide value can't silently wrap into a corrupt, possibly negative, result.
productionDeepDive.observability: Always handle strconv errors and log the offending input; a swallowed Atoi error turns malformed user input into a silent zero that's nearly impossible to trace later.
productionDeepDive.security: Treat all external numeric input as untrusted: validate ranges after parsing to prevent overflow-driven logic bypasses, and never trust string(n) to sanitize an integer into displayable text.

caseStudies.problem: int64 ids narrowed to int on 32-bit clients wrapped and collided.
caseStudies.solution: Serialize large ids as strings and parse with strconv.ParseInt, keeping them int64 end-to-end.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Slightly larger payloads and explicit parsing code for guaranteed correctness.
caseStudies.lessons: Make every narrowing boundary explicit and validated; never let a platform's int width silently truncate data.

keyTakeaways: Go has no implicit numeric conversions — write T(v) explicitly, even between int and int64.
float-to-int truncates toward zero (not rounds), and narrowing keeps only the low bits, wrapping predictably.
string(n) yields the rune for code point n, not its digits — use strconv.Itoa / strconv.Atoi for number<->text.
[]byte(s) and []rune(s) allocate and copy; type conversion (compile-time) is distinct from a type assertion (runtime on interfaces).
